idiom_name: ASP.NET Core policy authorization - [Authorize(Roles = "...")] or AddPolicy/RequireRole with a custom IAuthorizationRequirement + AuthorizationHandler; RoleManager<IdentityRole> for role CRUD
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core ships the RBAC primitives in the framework. The minimal realization is the role form: [Authorize(Roles = "Pauser,Admin")] on a controller or action, or a named policy built with AddAuthorization(o => o.AddPolicy("Pause", p => p.RequireRole("Pauser", "Admin"))) and referenced as [Authorize(Policy = "Pause")]. When a role is too coarse for the operation, declare an IAuthorizationRequirement and an AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement> that maps role claims to the required permission and succeeds only when satisfied - that handler is the decision point the authorization middleware consults before the action runs. Roles are data: IdentityRole rows managed through RoleManager<IdentityRole>, assigned with UserManager<TUser>.AddToRoleAsync, so a grant is one row change rather than a deploy. Authorization is deny-by-default only if configured: set a fallback policy (FallbackPolicy = a policy requiring an authenticated user, or a deny-everything policy) so an endpoint that forgets an attribute is closed, and drive roles from server-issued claims rather than anything the client sends.
pitfalls: Without a fallback policy every endpoint lacking an [Authorize] attribute is anonymous; set FallbackPolicy and test that an unannotated route is denied.
Role claims baked into a long-lived token keep a revoked role usable until expiry; keep tokens short with refresh or resolve roles server-side.
RequireRole("Admin") and the issued role claim must agree on casing and claim type; a mismatch fails closed (denies) or, with a custom handler, opens a hole.
Adding users directly to permissions instead of through roles recreates the group loophole; grant permissions only to roles.
A custom AuthorizationHandler that calls context.Succeed(requirement) without checking the requirement satisfies it unconditionally; make the handler's default outcome failure.
